prompt: At many universities, live lectures are being replaced by recorded material which students watch in their own time. Do you think this is a positive or a negative development?
essay:
The recorded lecture is usually discussed as a loss of contact, which assumes that the lecture was contact. Mostly it was not: several hundred people in a darkened room, listening in silence to a talk that will be given again next year in almost the same words. Moving it online is a positive development, and the reason is that it removes something whose value had already gone.

What a recording adds is control over the pace. A student can stop, look up an unfamiliar term, rewind the definition and go on, which is not a convenience but a substantial difference to how much is understood. It matters most to exactly the students who look weakest in a lecture hall: those working in a second language, those without the assumed background, those who simply need the sentence twice. The traditional format offered them nothing of the kind, and its defenders rarely mention them.

The genuine cost is not the disappearance of the lecture but the disappearance of what surrounded it. Turning up meant being seen to turn up, and a student who stopped coming used to be noticeable. It also meant the questions asked in the corridor afterwards, which is where most people discover that their confusion is shared. Those things were never the lecture, but they were attached to it, and they do not survive detachment on their own.

So the change is positive if the time it releases goes into the teaching that has to be live: small groups, argument, supervision, the parts a recording cannot carry. It is negative if institutions simply bank the saving. The technology has done the useful work by separating what could be broadcast from what could not, and whether that turns out well now depends entirely on what universities choose to do with the half they kept.
title: Recorded material replacing the live lecture
